summary: A position paper giving the cable television industry's viewpoint on requirements and selection criteria for the Next Generation of IP (IPng). It was written as input to the IETF's IPng selection effort and is informational only.

plainLanguage.summary: A cable TV group tells the people designing the next internet addresses what cable companies will need from them.

questions: what did cable tv want from the next ip
subtitle: Requirements for the next-generation IP from the cable television industry perspective.

tldr.problem: The cable television industry planned to deploy broadband networks supporting interactive video, voice, and data services to millions of homes simultaneously. These networks would have fundamentally different requirements (scale, real-time video, quality of service, security) than the research Internet of 1994.
tldr.mechanism: Time Warner Cable submitted this requirements paper to the IETF IPng selection process, detailing how the cable industry's vision of future broadband networks would challenge any next-generation IP protocol. Key requirements include resource reservation and flows (for video guarantees), policy-based routing (for differentiated services), accounting (for billing), error handling, and mobile host support.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 incorporated many of these ideas, including support for flows (IPv6 flow labels), quality of service capabilities, and authentication. However, the cable industry largely went a different path, using ATM and proprietary protocols rather than IP, until IP-based cable systems emerged decades later.

today: RFC 1686 presented an ambitious vision of broadband networks in 1994. IPv6 incorporated ideas from this and similar requirements papers, including flow labels and quality-of-service support. However, the cable industry did not primarily adopt IP for broadband delivery; instead, it developed proprietary and ATM-based systems. Decades later, IP-based cable systems (DOCSIS and others) emerged, making many of the RFC's visions practical.

sections.title: Cable Television Networks and Broadband Vision
sections.content:
In 1994, cable television networks passed approximately 90 million homes in the U.S. with about 56 million subscribers. The industry had installed over 1 million network-miles of cable infrastructure and was rapidly installing optical fiber. Cable companies were moving beyond simple television distribution to become integrated broadband networks supporting interactive video, voice, and data services.

The RFC describes the architecture of these networks: homes connect to fiber nodes via coaxial cable tree-and-branch plants, fiber nodes aggregate to headends where switching and routing equipment sits, and multiple headends connect to regional hub nodes over fiber optics. Cable networks were becoming two-way digital broadband systems with significant upstream bandwidth.

Time Warner's Full Service Network trial in Orlando exemplified the vision: each home received a set-top box (a powerful computer running broadband services), and the network delivered video on demand, interactive services, and data simultaneously. The authors positioned IP (or IPng) as a potential technology for these broadband networks, provided it could support the requirements of commercial, large-scale, quality-of-service-driven services.
sections.plainLanguage: Cable TV companies were planning to turn their networks into comprehensive broadband systems delivering TV, voice, and internet to homes. They wanted IPng to help, but they needed it to handle video reliably and support business operations.

sections.title: Technical Requirements for Broadband Networks
sections.content:
The RFC outlines engineering considerations for broadband networks. Scaling to 1012 nodes is needed globally; with roughly 1010 households worldwide, this leaves room for servers and other infrastructure. However, multiple addresses per household (for entertainment systems, computers, gaming devices) could stress the address space, and poor address administration could reduce effective availability.

Timescale was critical: the cable industry expected commercial deployment by 1998, meaning IPng definition and early implementations had to be available by 1995. Only with working prototypes could trials validate the technology. The RFC emphasizes that video quality is essential; demonstrating that IPng could carry real-time video and audio streams at scale would be decisive for adoption.

Transition and deployment must support both broadcast and multicast efficiently (for video distribution), real-time streams with bounded latency and jitter, and strong quality of service controls. Backwards compatibility with IPv4 is essential; a global Internet will remain heterogeneous with many IPv4 systems for a long time.

Mobile hosts will be common in future broadband networks. Mobility affects addressing, routing, resource reservation, security, and privacy.

Flows and resource reservation are essential: the bulk of broadband traffic will be real-time video and voice requiring performance guarantees for bandwidth, latency, jitter, and loss. The RFC notes that quality-of-service parameters vary by media type (MPEG-II video differs from G.721 PCM voice) and may require either soft or hard guarantees. Recovering from failed or lost resource reservations in distributed systems is challenging and requires care.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadband networks need huge addresses for all devices, early availability of IPng implementations so trials can start, video-quality assurance, backwards compatibility with old IP, support for mobile devices, and the ability to reserve bandwidth like airlines reserve airplane seats.

sections.title: Operational and Network Management Requirements
sections.content:
Configuration, administration and operation of large broadband networks is complex. Resource reservation, source routing, and quality of service control must interact carefully; there is tension between maintaining high QoS and low resource usage. Network operators need to monitor and direct traffic to meet quality and cost targets. The ability to dynamically reconfigure end-point connectivity (for mobile hosts or process migration) is important; normally, resources for new routes should be established before releasing the old route to minimize service interruption.

Policy-based routing allows the source or network operator to specify which network or route should carry traffic. Competing network operators and service providers want to offer differentiated services and customer lock-in through targeted service bundles. Information providers want to optimize content placement using point-to-point or selective multicast. This flexibility is attractive to the commercial broadband market.

Accounting is crucial for commercial networks. The ability to measure resource usage by user or session is required for billing and for operational planning. The RFC recommends efficient implementation that introduces minimal overhead.

Security must protect users' privacy (preventing traffic pattern analysis by examining packet headers) and protect network resources. The RFC notes that operators and information providers expect effective resource protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Commercial broadband networks need detailed tracking of who uses what (for billing), the ability to choose routing based on operator priorities (for service quality and business strategy), protection against spying on traffic, and careful management of network resources.

sections.title: Applicability and Technology Considerations
sections.content:
Applicability is broad: the cable industry targets homes as well as schools, business, and government campuses. Applications range from entertainment and remote education to telecommuting, medical services, and information access. Traffic will be dominated by real-time video and audio, though non-real-time services like messaging and file transfer remain important. IPng must be a general solution for diverse interactive multimedia applications, not just a research protocol.

Datagram service remains important but must be reexamined. The traditional best-effort, hop-by-hop IP service model may need enhancement to support resource reservation and quality of service guarantees for real-time traffic.

Support of communication media should be broad: IPng should not be locked to specific physical media but should generalize across diverse datalinks and support over any available communications medium.

Robustness and fault tolerance are essential. Service availability at expected performance levels is the true measure. Large networks with complex functions are vulnerable to bugs. The RFC warns that the change from IPv4 to IPng itself introduces risks; the design, implementation, and testing must be managed very carefully. New features like larger address space, source routing, and flows bring new failure modes that must be thoroughly tested.
sections.plainLanguage: IPng must work for every type of user and application, support video quality guarantees, work over any type of connection, and be rock-solid reliable in a network serving millions of homes.
